- [Stephane] Welcome
to the first deep dive
on an iterator service.
The first one is called IAM.
So IAM stands for identity
and access management.
It is a global service because in IAM,
we are going to create our
users and assign them to group.
So we've already used IAM without knowing,
when we created an account,
we created a root accounts,
and has been created by default.
This is the root user of our accounts.
And the only things you
should use it for is
to set up your account
as we'll do it right now.
But then you shouldn't
use that account anymore,
or even share it.
What you should be doing
instead, is create users.
So you will create users in IAM,
and one user represents one
person within your organization.
And the users can be grouped
together if it makes sense.
So let's take an example
we have an organization
with six people.
You have Alice, Bob,
Charles, David, Edward
and Fred so all these people
are in your organization.
Now Alice, Bob, and
Charles they work together.
They're all developers.
So we're going to create a group called
the group developers who regrouping Alice,
Bob and Charles.
And it turns out that David
and Edward also work together.
So we're going to create
an operations group.
Now we have two groups within IAM.
Now groups can only contain
users, not other groups.
So this is something very
important to understand.
Groups only contain users.
Now, some users don't
have to belong to a group.
For example, Fred right here is alone,
he does not correspond to any group.
That is not best practice.
But it is something you can do in AWS.
And also, a user can
belong to multiple groups.
That means that for example,
if you know that Charles
and David worked together,
and they're part of your audit team,
you can create a third group
with Charles and David.
And as you can see, now, in this example,
Charles and David are part
of two different groups.
So this is the possible
configurations for IAM.
So why do we create users
and why do we create groups?
Well, because we want to allow
them to use our AWS accounts
and to allow them to do so,
we have to give them permissions.
So users or groups can be assigned
what's called a JSON document.
I'll show you right now what
it means called a policy,
an IAM policy.
So it looks just like this.
So you don't have to be a programmer.
This is not programming.
This is just describing
in, I think plain English,
what a user is allowed
to do or what a group
and all the users within
that group are allowed to do.
So in this example, we can
see that we allow people
to use the EC2 to service

to use the elastic load balancing service

and to use CloudWatch.
Now we'll see what EC2
elastic load balancing
and CloudWatch mean, but
through this JSON document
that looks just like this.
We are allowing our users
to use some services in AWS.
So these policies will
help us define permissions
of our users.
And so in AWS, you don't allow
everyone to do everything
that would be catastrophic,
because a new user could
basically launch so many services
and they will cost you a lot of money
or would be valid for security.
So in AWS, you apply a principle called
the least privilege principle.
So you don't give more
permissions than a user needs.
Okay, so if a user just needs
access to three services,
just create a permission for that user.
So now we have seen an overview IAM.

--- EC2 Placement Groups ---

1
So now, let's talk about placement groups.
2
Placement groups are a little bit more advanced,
3
and we wanna use them once,
4
we want to have control over how our EC2 instances
5
are going to be placed within the AWS infrastructure.
6
So that strategy can be defined
7
using these placement groups.
8
So we don't get direct interaction with the hardware of AWS,
9
but we let AWS know how we would like our EC2 instance
10
to be placed compared to one another.
11
So when you create a placement group,
12
you have three strategies available for you.
13
You have the cluster placement group in which your instances
14
will be grouped together in a low-latency hardware setup
15
within a single availability zone.
16
This is going to give you high performance but high risk.
17
We'll see this in details in a second.
18
Spread means that your instances
19
are going to be spread across different hardware,
20
and there is a restriction on this.
21
That means you can only have seven EC2 instance
22
per placement group that spread per AZ.
23
So you would use a spread placement group
24
when you have critical applications.
25
Finally, the last one is a new kind
26
of placement group that is really helpful.
27
It's called partition.
28
It's similar to the spread,
29
meaning that you want to spread your instances,
30
but here, they're spread across many different partitions.
31
And these partitions rely on different sets of racks
32
of hardware within an AZ.
33
What does that mean is that they're still spread,
34
but they're not isolated one from another failure,
35
but a partition should be isolated
36
from another partition of failure.
37
The idea with this is that you can scale to hundreds
38
of EC2 instances per group, and that allows you
39
to run applications such as Hadoop,
40
Cassandra, or Kafka.
41
Now, let's have a look into each
42
of these placement groups in details.
43
So next, we have the cluster placement group,
44
and all your EC2 instances are going to be
45
in the same availability zone.
46
So why do we do this?
47
Well, this particular placement group
48

So you have around 10 gigabits per second
50
of bandwidth between all these instances

that will have enhanced networking enabled.

And so you get low latency, high throughput network.
53
And the idea is that out of this,
54
you can get great performance
55
for any kind of computational job.
56
So a drawback of using this architecture
57
is that if your availability zone fails,
58
then all the instances will fail at the same time.
59
But usually, for use case, this is fine.
60
So the use cases for this kind of placement group
61
are big data jobs that need to complete very fast
62
with very high networking
63
or applications that need extremely low latency
64
and high throughput network
65
between each instance of your application.
66
Now, spread is the complete opposite.
67
In spread, we want to minimize the failure risk.

And so in this case, when we ask for spread placement group,
69
all the EC2 instances are going to be located

on different hardware.

So as you can see here, we have three AZ,

and we have six EC2, and each EC2 instance

is on a different hardware.

So what does that mean?

Well, what we get is that we can span across multiple AZ,

and there is a reduced risk of simultaneous failure.

Why?

Well, because if my hardware one fails,

I'm pretty sure my hardware two will not fail.

And so we've separated the risk

of my two instances in the Us-east-1a

to fail at the same time.

And so that's the benefit from it.

The con is that from this configuration,

we're limited to seven instances per AZ per placement group.
86
So there is a limit to how big your placement group can be.
87
And so you need to have application
88
that's gonna be of good size but not too big.
89
The use case would be an application that needs to maximize
90
high availability and reduce the risk.
91
And in general, for critical applications
92
where your instance failures must be isolated
93
from one another.
94
Remember, here, we have a limitation
95
of seven instances per AZ per placement group.
96
Now, for the partition placement group,
97
we can have instances spread across partitions
98
in multiple available T-zones.
99
So we can have up to seven partitions per AZ.

So in this example, we have partition one
101
and partition two in us-east-1a

and partition three in us-east-1b.

And on each partition, you can have many EC2 instances.

So in the first one have four,

and the second one have four,

and the third one have four as well.

So why do we use a partition placement group?

Well, each partition represents a rack in AWS.
109
And so by having many partitions, you're making sure
110
that your instances are distributed
111
across many hardware racks, and so therefore,
112
they're safe from a rack failure from one another.

So you can have up to seven partitions per AZ,

and these partitions can span

across multiple availability zones in the same region.

You can get up to hundreds of EC2 instances with the setup.

So this is a difference

versus the spread type of placement group.

And as I said, the instances in the partition

do not share the same hardware physical rack

with the instances in the other partitions,

and therefore, each partition is isolated from failure.

So that means that, yes, if one goes down,

if partition goes down, the partition number two,

then partition number one should be fine.

And to know which partition these EC2 instances are on,

there is an option to access this information

with using the metadata service.

So when would you use a partition placement group?

Well, when you have an application

that it can be partition aware to distribute the data

and your servers across partitions.

And usually, the use cases
134
are going to be big data applications

--- EC2 Hibernate ---

1
So let's talk about a lesser-known feature
2
called EC2 Hibernate.
3
So we know that we can stop and terminate instances,
4
and when we do so, when we stop it,
5
the data on disk, on your EBS disk,
6
is going to be kept intact until the next start.
7
That makes sense.
8
And if we terminate it, well,
9
if you set up the root volume
10
to be destroyed with your instance,
11
it's going to be destroyed,
12
but any volume that is not set up to be destroyed
13
when your instance is terminated will be kept.
14
And then when you start an instance,
15
well, the OS, the operating system will boot
16
and then the EC2 User Data that was going to be run,
17
the script, and then the OS will boot up.
18
And then your application starts, your caches get warmed,
19
and that can take time,
20
because you are booting your machine, right?
21
But the idea is that with Hibernate,
22
we want to achieve a new state.
23
So when we hibernate an instance, whatever was in RAM,
24
the in-memory state is going to be preserved.
25
What does that mean?
26
That means that your instance boot is going
27
to be much faster,
28
because the operating system is not stopped or restarted,
29
the operating system is actually just frozen,
30
it's hibernated.
31
And under the hood, well,
32
whatever was in the RAM state is going to be written
33
into a file in the root EBS volume.
34
So that means that the root EBS volume must be encrypted
35
and that it must have enough space to contain the RAM.
36
So let me show you what happens.
37
So we take an EC2 instance,
38
and it's running and there is data in RAM,
39
and then we start a hibernation process.
40
So what happens that the instance will go
41
in the stopping state,
42
and the RAM is going to be dumped into your EBS volume.
43
Then the instance is shut down and the RAM disappears,
44
because as soon as you stop an instance the RAM goes away,
45
but the EBS volume still contains the dump of the RAM.
46
And then when your instance is started,
47
then the RAM is going to be loaded from disk
48
onto the EC2 instance memory.
49
And that means that it is just as is
50
your EC2 instance never got stopped.
51
And we'll have a look at this in the hands-on.
52
So the use cases for hibernation is
53
if you want to have long-running processes
54
and never actually stop them,
55
or if you want to save the RAM state,
56
or if you just want to reboot, like boot up fast,
57
and you have services that take time to initialize.
58
So you actually don't want them to initialize,
59
you want them to stay up and running
60
even if you hibernate your instance.
61
So, some good things to know about EC2 Hibernate is that
62

--- EBS Overview ---

Welcome to this section where we will look at the different storage options for EC2 instances.
So first the most important ones are going to be EBS volumes.
So let's define what they are.
And EBS volume stands for Elastic Block Store.
It's a network drive that you can attach to your instances while they run.
And we've been using them without even knowing.
So we this EBS volumes allow us to persist data even after the instance is terminated.
And so that's the whole purpose.
We can recreate an instance and mount the same EBS volume from before, and we will get back our data.
That is very helpful.
So these EBS volumes at the CCP level can only be mounted to one instance at a time.
Okay.
And when you create an EBS volume it is bound to a specific availability zone.
That means that you cannot have an EBS volume in created in, for example, US East one attached to
an instance in US east one b.
We'll see this in the diagram in a second.
So how do you think of EBS volumes.
Well you can think of them as network USB sticks.
So it's a USB stick that you can take from a computer and put it in another computer, but you actually
don't physically put it in a computer.
It's attached through the network.
Now let's look at it.
So EBS volumes are network drive.
As I said it's not a physical drive okay.
So to communicate between the instance and the EBS volume it will be using the network.
And because the network is used there may be a bit of latency from one computer to reach to another
server.
Now EBS volumes, because they are a network drive, they can be detached from an EC2 instance and attached
to another one very quickly.
And that makes it super handy when you want to do failovers.
For example, EBS volumes are locked to a specific availability zones.
That means that, as I said, if it's created in Us-east-1, it cannot be attached to Us-east-1.
But we will see in this section that if we do a snapshot, then we are able to move a volume across
from different availability zones.
And finally it's a volume.
So you have to provision capacity in advance.
So you need to say how many gigabytes you want in advance.
And the IOPs which is I o operations per second.
And you're basically defining how you want your EBS volume to perform.
You're going to get billed for that provisioned capacity.
And you can increase the capacity over time if you want to have better performance or more size.
So as a diagram, what does it look like?
Well we have usd1 a we have one EC2 instance.
And we can attach for example one EBS volume to that EC2 instance.
If we create another EC2 instance, as I said, an EBS volume cannot be attached to two instances at
a time at the certified cloud practitioner level.
And therefore, what I want to say is that this EC2 instance needs to have its own EBS volume attached
to it, but it is very possible for us to have two EBS volumes attached to one instance.
Think of it as two network USB sticks into one machine.
That makes a lot of sense.
Now EBS volumes are linked to an availability zone.
So as you can see, all this diagram has been so far using US East one.
So if you wanted to have other EBS volumes in another AZ, then you would need to create this separately
in the other availability zone.
So just the same way that your EC2 instances are bound to an AZ, so are the EBS volumes.
Finally, it is possible for us to create EBS volumes and leave them unattached.
They don't need to be necessarily attached to an EC2 instance.
They can be attached on demand and that makes it very, very powerful.
Finally, when we go ahead and create EBS volumes, uh, through EC2 instances, there is this thing
called a delete on termination attribute.
And this can come up in the exam.
So if you look at this when we create an EBS volume in the console, when we create an EC2 instance,
there is the second to last column called delete on termination.
And by default it is ticked for the root volume and not ticked for a new EBS volume.
So this controls the EBS behavior when an EC2 instance is being terminated.
So by default, as you can see, the EBS volume is deleted alongside the instance being terminated.
So it's enabled.
And by default any other attached EBS volume is not deleted because it's disabled by default.
But obviously, as we can see in this UI, we can control if you want to enable or disable delete on
termination.
And so use case for.
It would be for example that if you want to preserve the root volume when an instance is terminated,
for example to save some data, then you can disable delete on termination for the root volume and you'll
be good to go.
And that could be an exam scenario at the exam.
So I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

from one AZ to another.

Next, you need to know about a few EBS Snapshots feature.
18

19
It's the ability for you to move the snapshot
20
to an "archive tier" that is going to be up to 75% cheaper.
21

22

23
for restoring the archive.

The last feature you need to know about

--- Elastic Load Balancer - Connection Draining ---

1
So now let's talk about a feature
2
that can come up in the exam,
3
which is called Connection Draining.
4
So it has two names, actually.
5
If you're using a Classic Load Balancer,
6
it is called Connection Draining,
7
but if you're using an Application Balancer
8
or a Network Load Balancer,
9
this is called a Deregistration Delay.
10
And the idea behind this concept is that
11
it will give some time for your instances
12
to complete the inflight request or the active request
13
while the instance is being deregistered
14
or marked unhealthy.
15
And once a connection is being drained,
16
so once an instance is being drained,
17
then the ELB will stop sending your request
18
to the EC2 instance that is being drained
19
while being deregistered.
20
So let's have a look at a diagram to understand better.
21
So we have three EC2 instances
22
and in one of them we'll set it in draining mode.
23
So the users that are already connected to that EC2 instance
24
are going to be given enough time,
25
which is the draining period, okay,
26
to complete their existing connection
27
and to complete their existing request.
28
And then once everything's done,
29
then all the connections will be shut down.
30
Now, if new users try to connect to our ELB,
31
our ELB is smart enough to know
32
that because our EC2 instance is in draining state,
33
then it will only establish new connections
34
with other EC2 instances, for example,
35
my second EC2 instance or my third EC2 instance.
36
Now you can parametrize
37
these Connection Draining parameters.
38
So you can set it anywhere between 1 to 3,600 seconds.
39
By default, it is 300 seconds, so five minutes,
40
and you can disable it altogether
41
if you set the value to zero,
42
which means that there's no draining happening.
43
Now, if you set it to low value, okay, this is good
44
if your requests are short, for example, if there were very,
45
very short requests for, let's say, less than one second,
46
well, it's a good idea to set
47
the draining connection parameter to maybe 30 seconds, okay,
48
because then this will allow your EC2 instance
49
to be drained really fast and then be taken offline,
50
maybe to be replaced or something like this.
51
If your request can be quite long, for example,
52
if you have uploads or long lived requests,
53
then you want to set it to something pretty high,
54
but the trade-off is that's your EC2 instance
55
is not going to go away as soon as soon as possible, okay,
56
it's going to have to wait
57
until this Connection Draining period is done, okay?
58
So this is what you need to know about this setting
59
at a high level.
60
I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

2

--- Auto Scaling Groups - Scaling Policies ---

1
So we have several scaling policies
2
for auto scaling group.
3
The first one is dynamic scaling and within this category,
4
we have the target tracking scaling,
5

The idea is that you define a metric for your ASG,
7

16
to your auto scaling group.

18

19

20

21

the minimum capacity to 10.

--- Route 53 - TTL ---

1
Okay, so let's have a look at TTLs.
2
So a record TTL is a Time To Live.
3
And let's take this example where a client is accessing
4
our DNS Route 53 and a web server.
5
So we do a DNS request for myapp.example.com,
6
and we get an answer from the DNS,
7
which is saying, hey, please, this is an A record.
8
Here is the IP, and there is a TTL,
9
maybe a TTL of 300 seconds.
10
So TTL is saying, hey clients, please cache this result
11
for the duration of the TTL.
12
So for 300 seconds,
13
the client is going to cache the results.
14
That means that if the client is requesting again
15
or accessing the same host name,
16
what's going to happen is that
17
the client will not issue a query to the DNS system,
18
because it already knows the answer,
19
because the answer has been cached,
20
and we're still within the cache period, so the cache TTL.
21
The idea behind this
22
is that we don't want to query the DNS too often,
23
because we don't expect records to change a lot,
24
and so, therefore, using the response it has,
25
the client can access our web server
26
and do HTTP request and responses.
27
So we have, you know, two extreme cases.
28
For example, if you set a high TTL of, say, 24 hours,
29
then this is going to do a lot less traffic on Route 53,
30
because less clients are doing requests,
31
because the result are cached for 24 hours,
32
and, possibly, while the client will have outdated records.
33
If somehow you want to change the record,
34
you will need to wait 24 hours
35
to make sure that all your clients
36
will have the new records in their cache.
37
If you said set a low TTL,
38
for example, 60 seconds, at the opposite,
39
then it's going to do a lot more traffic on your DNS,
40
so a lot more dollar you're going to spend,
41
because you get price per how many request
42
do reach Route 53.
43
But the records will be outdated for less time,
44
so it's quicker for you to do a record change,
45
and it's easier to change records overall.
46
So it's up to you, really,
47
to see what a good TTL or low TTL is.
48
If you plan on changing a record,
49
the idea is that sometimes
50
you will decrease the TTL for, say, 24 hours,
51
and then when you know that all the clients
52
have a new TTL that is low,
53
then you change the record value
54
which gets updated for everyone,
55
and then you increase the TTL.
56
This is a strategy.
57
So the TTL is mandatory for every record
58
except the Alias record that we'll see in the next lecture.
59
So let's have a look how TTL works in the console.

--- Route 53 CNAME vs Alias ---

1
So now let's have a look at the differences
2
between CNAME and Aliases.
3
So when you have an AWS Resource,
4
for example, a Load Balancer or CloudFront,
5
it will expose a hostname.
6
And what you want is to maybe map that hostname
7
to a domain you own.
8
For example, you want to map this Load Balancer
9
into myapp.mydomain.com.
10
So we have two options.
11
The first one is to use a CNAME record.
12
So we've seen A records,
13
but now let's look at CNAME records.
14
So CNAME allows you to point a hostname
15
to any other hostname.
16
For example, you can say app.mydomain.com
17
is pointing to blabla.anything.com.
18
And this only works if you have a non root domain name,
19
so if you have something.mydomain.com.
20
It does not work for just mydomain.com,
21
as we'll see in the hands-on.
22
On the other hand, you have alias records,
23
and these are specific to Route 53,
24
but they allow you to point a hostname
25
to a specific AWS Resource.
26
So app.mydomain.com is pointing to blabla.amazonaws.com.
27
And these resources we'll see in a second where they are.
28

--- Route 53 Resolvers & Hybrid DNS ---

1
Okay, so let's have a little talk
2
about the Route 53 Resolver.
3
So the idea is that by default,
4
when you have a Route 53 Resolver,
5
which is the basic thing you create in Route 53
6
when you start using it,
7
it will answer DNS queries
8
for the local domain names for your EC2 instances
9
for the records in your private hosted zones,
10
as well as for the records in your public name server.
11
So everything you create under Route 53
12
is going to be answered within your account.
13
But you may want to have a situation
14
where you want a hybrid DNS.
15
That means that you want this resolver to resolve
16
as well the DNS of your own network and vice versa.
17
So you want to establish connectivity
18
between your AWS Cloud DNS
19
and the DNS of your on-premises network.
20
And so how do we do this?
21
For this, we're going to use what's called
22
a Resolver endpoint.
23
So this is just a simplified version,
24
but the idea is that we're going
25
to create an inbound endpoint
26
that will allow the DNS resolvers of on-premises resources
27
to resolve domain names of AWS resources.
28
So how does that work?
29
Say we have established
30
our own Route 53 Resolver in our cloud
31
and we have an EC2 instance, a private hosted zone,
32
and we have our on-premises data center.
33
A server on it is going to be, first of all,
34
we need to establish of course,
35
connectivity between our data center and AWS
36
using a VPN or a direct connect connection.
37
And then this server is going to do a DNS query,
38
for example, to look for a domain name
39
that belongs to our private hosted zone,
40
is going to be passed to the closest DNS resolver,
41
so the on-premises resolver,
42
and these resolver are going to be set up to talk
43
to a resolver inbound endpoint,
44
and to pass on this DNS query into our AWS Cloud.
45
And this resolver knows how to talk
46
to the Route 53 Resolver.
47
So this is how you have the full chain
48
of lookups from your on-premises data center
49
to your cloud using an inbound endpoint.
50
And of course you can do it the other way
51
with an outbound endpoint in which your Route 53 Resolver
52
will forward DNS queries to your resolver on-premises.
53
So again, if we have a look,
54
we have the two infrastructures that are connected,
55
and then we're going to have a resolver outbound endpoint.
56
And this time whenever you EC2 instance queries
57
for a DNS query that is resolved on-premises,
58
for example, web.onpremise.private,
59
is going to be passed through the resolver outbound endpoint
60
to the DNS resolvers of the on-premises data center,
61
and we'll be good to go.
62
So that's it.
63
The idea behind this, I think, a bit complicated lecture
64
is that if you want to connect
65
your on-premises data center and AWS
66
and make sure the DNS queries are resolved both ways,
67
you must use the resolver inbound and outbound endpoint.

And that's about it. All you should know.

--- S3 Overview ---

1
Welcome to this section on Amazon S3.
2
So this section is very important
3
because Amazon S3 is one of the main building blocks of AWS.
4
And the way it's advertised
5
is that it's infinitely scaling storage.
6
So as a matter of fact,
7
a lot of the web relies on Amazon S3.
8
For example, many websites use Amazon S3 as a backbone,

for integrations as well.

to learn the main features.

So there are so many use cases for Amazon S3
15
because at its core, it is storage.
16
So Amazon S3 is used for backup and storage.
17
It could be for your files,
18
it could be for your disk and so on.
19
For disaster recovery purposes,
20
for example, you'll move your data to another region.
21
In case a region goes down,
22
then your data is backed up somewhere else.
23
It's for archival purposes.
24
So you can archive files in Amazon S3
25
and retrieve it at a later stage for much, much cheaper.
26
For hybrid cloud storage,
27
so in case you have storage on premises,
28
but you won't expand it into the cloud,
29
you can use Amazon S3 for this.
30
To host applications, to host media such as video files,
31
images, and so on,
32
to have a data lake to store a lot of data
33
and to perform big data analytics,
34
for delivering software updates
35
for hosting static websites, and so on.

And two use cases is that the NASDAQ
37

which is like the archival service of Amazon S3.

And Sysco runs analytics
40
on its data and gains business insights from Amazon S3.

So now, let's talk about the bucket.
42
So Amazon S3 allows people to store objects
43
or files into buckets.
44
They're directories within the cloud.
45
And the buckets are defined at the region level.
46
So you say you create a buckets for a specific AWS region.
47
Even though S3 has a global interface
48
in which you'll be able to see all the buckets
49
from all the regions,
50
the buckets themselves are assigned to a specific region.
51
Now, for the naming, there is something that you should know
52
that is quite recent and new.
53
So it used to be that Amazon S3
54
needed to have buckets with a globally unique name.
55
That means that the name for your S3 bucket belong to you
56
and no one else could use it across the world,
57
across all the regions, across all the accounts.
58
But now, there is a new feature
59
to have an account regional namespace,
60
and it allows you to reuse the same bucket name
61
across the regions for all your accounts and so on,
62
even though someone else may have named
63
the bucket the same way because AWS will add a suffix
64
to your bucket name,
65
making sure that it's going to be unique anyway.
66
So naming constraints, you have no uppercase,
67
no underscore, not an IP.
68
It must start with a lowercase number or letter,
69
it must not start with a prefix XN,
70
and it must not end with a suffix minus S3 alias.
71
So overall, you're completely fine
72
if you use letters and numbers and you keep it simple.
73
And before there was a constraint
74
around the global unique name,
75
but now with the account original namespace,
76
you can pretty much use whatever you want
77
for your bucket name in AWS, which is super nice.

Okay, so now let's talk about objects.

--- S3 Security: Bucket Policy ---

1
So now let's talk about Amazon S3-Security.
2
The first part is User-Based.
3
So as a user you can have IAM policies that you
4
and this IAM policy is going to authorize
5
which API calls should be allowed for a specific IAM user.
6
You can also have Resource-Based Security.
7
So this is new.
8
We can use what's called S3 Bucket policies
9
and there are bucket wide rules
10
that you can assign directly from the S3 console.
11
And this will allow, for example, a specific user to come in
12
or allow a user from another account,
13
this is called cross-account
14
to access your S3 Buckets.
15
This is also how we'll make our S3 Buckets public
16
as I will show you in a minute.
17
Next, you have the Object Access Control List or ACL,
18
they're finer grain security and they can be disabled.
19
And if you need to go
20
at the Bucket level, you can have Buckets ACL
21
which is way less common also can be disabled.
22
And the most common way now to do security
23
on an Amazon S3 Bucket is to use Bucket policies.
24
So in which situation can an IAM principle
25
can access an S3 object?
26
Well, if the IAM permissions allow it
27
or if the resource policies allows it
28
and that there is no explicit deny in the action,
29
then the IAM principle can access the S3 object
30
on the specified API call.
31
So we'll have a look at these use cases in a minute.
32
Finally, another way to do security on Amazon S3
33
is to encrypt the objects using encryption keys.
34
So what does S3 Bucket policy actually look like?
35
Because this is the focus of S3-Security for us.
36
So they are JSON based policies and they look like this.
37
So this is JSON documents and it's quite easy to read.
38
So the first thing is that you have a resource block
39
and the resource tells the policy
40
what buckets and object this policy applies on.
41
And in here we can see that this applies to every object
42
within the example Bucket,
43
this is what the star is for.
44
Next we have the effect.
45
So Allow or Deny, and what do we Allow or Deny?
46

--- S3 Versioning ---

1
So, now let's talk about versioning
2
in Amazon S3.
3
Because we've seen how to create a website,
4
but it would be nice to be able to update it in a safe way.
5
So, you can version your files in Amazon S3,
6
and this is a setting you have to enable
7
at the bucket level.
8
So, we have my bucket and it's enabled with versioning.
9
So, whenever a user uploads a file,
10
it's going to create a version of that file
11
at the selected key.
12
And then should we re-upload the same key,
13
should we overwrite that file,
14
then instead it's going to create a version two,
15
and then a version three, and so on.
16
So, therefore, it is best practice to version your buckets.
17
Why?
18
Well, the first thing is that it protects
19
against unintended deletes.
20
So, for example, if you delete a file version,
21
actually you just add a delete marker
22
and therefore you can restore versions
23
that were previously there instead.
24
You can also easily roll back to a previous version.
25
So, if you want to go back to what happened two days ago,
26
you can take a file and roll it back.
27
So, there are some notes you need to be aware of.
28
First of all, that any file that is not versioned
29
prior to enabling versioning will have the version null.
30
And also that if you suspend versioning,
31
it does not delete the previous version,
32
so, it's a safe operation.
33
Okay, so now let's go into the console
34
and have a look at how we can use versioning.

--- S3 Replication ---

1
Now let's talk about Amazon S3 Replication,
2
and there are two flavors of it.
3
So CRR is for cross-region replication
4
and SRR is for same-region replication.
5
The idea is that we have an S3 Bucket in one region
6
and a target S3 Bucket in another region,
7
and we want to set up asynchronous replication
8
between these two buckets.
9
So, to do so, we first must enable Versioning
10
in the source and the destination buckets.
11
And if we do CRR, so cross-region replication,
12
the two regions must be different.
13
If we do SRR, the two regions are the same.
14
Now, it's possible for you to have these buckets
15
in different AWS accounts
16
and copying happens asynchronously.
17
So the replication mechanism happens behind the scenes,
18
in the background.
19
And to make replication work,
20
you must give proper IAM permissions
21
to the S3 service so that it has the permission
22
to read and write from specified buckets.
23
So the use cases for replication are manyfold.
24
The first one is that if you use cross-region replication,
25
this can be helpful for compliance
26
or for providing lower latency access to your data
27
because it's in another region,
28
or to replicate data across accounts.
29
For SRR, or same-region replication,
30
this can be very helpful to aggregate logs
31
across multiple S3 Buckets
32
or to perform a live replication
33
between a production and test accounts,
34
so, you have your own test environment.
35
Okay, so that's it about replication.
36
I will see you in the next lecture for some practice.

--- S3 Replication Notes ---

1
Hey, so just a few notes
2
about Amazon S3 Replications.
3
So after you enable Replication, as you've seen,
4
only new objects are going to be replicated.
5
And if you want to replicate existing objects,
6
then you need to use the S3 Batch Replication feature.
7
So this will replicate the existing objects
8
and the objects that have failed Replication,
9
and in case you have delete operations,
10
you can replicate these delete markers
11
from the source bucket to the target bucket.
12
It's an optional setting, but if you have a deletion
13
with the version ID, they are not replicated,
14
so if it's a permanent deletion,
15
because you want to avoid malicious deletes happening
16
from one bucket to another.
17
Finally, there's no chaining of replications.
18
So that means that if bucket one
19
has replication to bucket two,
20
and then, bucket two has replication to bucket three,
21
then the objects of bucket one
22
are not replicated into the bucket three, so that's it.
23
I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

--- S3 Encryption ---

1
So now let's talk about object encryption

So the first one is Amazon S3 for SSE-S3 encryption.

and then you're gonna get encryption,

So now to read that file from the S3 bucket,

to encrypt this object.

So this is another level of security.

So this is something the exam may test you on.

Next we have the SSE-C type of encryption.

the encryption key you provide.

113
and then put the file as encrypted into an S3 bucket.
114
And of course, to read that file,
115
the user must again provide the key

that was used to encrypt that file.

Finally, we have the client-side encryption.

So this is easier to implement

if we leverage some client library
120
such as the Client-Side Encryption Library.
121
And the idea with client-side encryption
122
is that the clients must encrypt data themselves
123

And also, you can retrieve the data from Amazon S3,

and then the decryption of the data happens
126

So how does that work?

We have a file and we have a client's key

that's outside of AWS.

The client itself is going to provide
133
and perform the encryption,

so now we have an encrypted file,

and that file as is can be sent into Amazon S3 for upload.
136
So we've seen all the levels of encryption of objects,
137
but now let's talk about encryption in transit.
138
So encryption in transit, or in flight,
139
is also called SSL or TLS,
140
and basically your Amazon S3 bucket has two endpoints,
141
the HTTP endpoint that is not encrypted
142
and the HTTPS endpoint that has encryption in flights.

So anytime you visit a website

and you see that green lock or lock,

usually that means it's using encryption in flights,
146
meaning the connection between you
147
and the target server is secure and fully encrypted.

Therefore, when you're using Amazon S3,

it's fully recommended to use HTTPS

to have secure transmission of data, of course,

and if you use the SSE-C type of mechanism,

you must use the HTTPS protocol.

Now this is not something to worry about in real life

--- S3 Pre-signed URLs ---

1
So, now, let's talk about
2

3
So, they are URLs you can generate using the S3 console,
4
the CLI or the SDK, and the URL has an expiration.
5
So if you use the console, it's up to 12 hours
6
and if use the CLI, you can go up to 168 hours.
7
So, the idea is that when you generate a pre-signed URL,
8
the user that will get that URL will inherit the permissions
9
of the user that generated that URL for a GET or a PUT.
10
So what's the use case?
11
Well, say you have an S3 bucket and it's private,
12
and you want to give someone outside of AWS
13
access to one file.
14
You don't want to make that file public.
15
You don't want to make that file in any way
16
that would break your security, right?
17
So, you as your bucket owner or the user,
18
you're going to generate a pre-signed URL out of this file,
19
and the S3 Bucket will give you a URL.
20
That URL is going to be pre-signed,
21
meaning that it will carry over your credentials,
22
in terms of authorization to access that file.
23
Then you will send this URL to the target user
24
that you want to give access to the file
25
for a limited amount of time.
26
And then that user, sorry,
27
will be using the URL to access the file
28
on the S3 Buckets.
29
And then you will get a file back from the S3 buckets,
30
and the user has being able to download it, for example.
31
So, pre-signed URL are a very, very common use case
32
when it comes to temporary access to one specific file
33
for download or even for upload.
34
So, the examples are to only allow logged-in users
35
to download a premium video of your S3 bucket
36
or to allow an ever-changing list of users
37
to download files by generating URLs dynamically,
38
or to allow, temporarily, a user to upload a file
39
to a precise location in your S3 bucket,

--- Glacier Vault Lock & S3 Object Lock ---

1
So now let's talk about S3 Glacier Vault Lock.
2
So the idea is that you want to lock your Glacier Vault
3
to adapt a WORM model.
4
That means Write Once Read Many.
5
So the idea is that you take an object,
6

7

8

9

11

12
That means that once you've set a Vault Lock
13
Policy and you locked it,
14

15

16
So that means that once an object is inserted into your
17
Glacier vault and the vault itself has a Vault Lock Policy
18

19

21

But some users, the admin users,

--- CloudFront Overview ---

1
Now let's talk about CloudFront.
2
CloudFront is a content delivery network or CDN.
3
So anytime you see CDN in the exam, think CloudFront.
4
It improves the read performance by caching the content
5
of your website at the different edge locations.
6
And because your content is cached all around the world,
7
then your users all around the world
8
will have a lower latency
9
and this will improve the user experience.
10
CloudFront is made of hundreds of
11
points of presence globally and that includes
12
edge locations and caches across the world.
13
On top of it, by having the content distributed globally,
14
we are getting DDoS protection.
15
So DDoS is a sort of attack where all your servers
16
around the world are getting attacked at the same time.
17
We'll see this later on in this course,
18
and the idea is that CloudFront,
19
because your application is worldwide,
20
then you're protected against these attacks
21
also using something called Shield
22
and Web Application Firewall
23
that we will be seeing in the security section.
24
So if you wanna look at a map of the world,
25
these are the map and we see some edge locations
26
as well as edge caches.
27
And so say we had created an S3 bucket
28
and a website on our S3 bucket in Australia,
29
but we had a user maybe in America.
30
Then what the user will do is that
31
it will request the content
32
from an American edge location using CloudFront
33
and CloudFront will be able to fetch
34
the content from Australia.
35
Now, if another user in the US
36
will be requesting the same content,
37
then it will be served directly from the edge
38
and it will not go all the way to Australia
39
to serve that content.
40
Same if a user is in China, then it'll be talking
41
to a Chinese point of presence
42

--- CloudFront - Cache Invalidation ---

1
So now, let's talk about cache invalidations
2
in CloudFront.
3
So, CloudFront has a backend origin,

of course.

from your backend origin, the update you want,

once the TTL of the cache has expired.

16
present in your cache.

And to this, you too,
18
perform what's called a CloudFront invalidation.

So, you can either invalidate all the files with a star
21
or invalidate a special path,

for example, /images/*.

Okay, so how does that work?
24
Well, say we have a CloudFront distribution,

two edge locations.

30
the TTL for these files are set to one day.

32
the edge locations will re-fetch these files for the cache.

Now, you as a user,
34
you're an admin, you're going to update the files

--- AWS Snow Family Overview ---

1
Okay, so now let's talk about AWS Snowball.
2
So it's a highly secure and portable device
3
that allows you to collect and process data
4
at the edge and migrate data in and out of AWS.
5
So if you have a migration of say, petabytes of data,
6
Snowball may be a good use case.
7
So we have two kind of Snowball edge devices.
8
One is called the Edge Storage Optimized,
9
and the other one is called the Edge Compute Optimized.
10
And the difference lies in their storage.
11
As you can see, one has 210 terabytes
12
and the other one has 28 terabytes.
13
So obviously one is for storage
14
and the other one is only used for computer.
15
So let me tell you about data migrations.
16
So it takes a lot of time to transfer some data
17
over a specific bandwidth speed.
18
For example, if you want to transfer a hundred terabytes
19
over one gigabytes per second connection,
20
it would take you 12 days.
21
So when you have a slow connection,
22
you may have limited connectivity, limited bandwidth,
23
very high network cost, and you have to share the bandwidth,
24
for example, with some other applications,
25
the connection may not be stable.
26
So whenever you have these kind of challenges,
27
or if it takes you, for example, over a week
28
to transfer data over the network,
29
the recommendation is to use a Snowball device.
30
So the idea is that if you upload directly to Amazon S3,
31
it's simple, but it may use all your bandwidth.
32
And if you use Snowball,
33
well, you're going to receive a physical Snowball device,
34
you, yourself in your own infrastructure.
35
So it's a physical machine,
36
and then you load it with the data you need,
37
and then finally you ship it back to AWS.
38
And then you will be having an export process
39
within AWS to take your data from the Snowball onto,
40
for example, an Amazon S3 bucket.
41
So this is the main use case of a Snowball device.
42
The other one is a edge computing use case.
43
So the idea is that you wanna process data
44
while it's being created on an edge location.
45
For example, it's a truck on the road or a ship on the sea,
46
or a mining station on the ground.
47
And these locations may have no internet access
48
or limited access to internet or compute power.
49
So here again, we order one of these
50
big Snowball edge devices and we do edge computing.
51
And so that means that we have the Compute Optimized,
52
this is dedicated for that use case

for the search optimized devices.
54
And then because they have computing capability,
55
we can actually run EC2 instances
56
or Lambda functions directly on these devices.

The idea is that once the data is created
58
and processed, we can send it back again to AWS,

but by using an edge computing device,
60
we can pre-process the data
61
or we can do machine learning at the edge
62
or directly transcode media at the edge.
63
And that's the use case for edge computing.
64
So hopefully that makes sense.

The Snowball service is really just something that is used

--- SQS - Message Visibility Timeout ---

1
So now let's talk about an important concept,
2
which is called the message visibility timeout.
3
So when a message is polled by a consumer,
4
it becomes invisible to other consumers.
5
So let's take an example.
6
We have the time going from left to right,
7
and we have a consumer doing a ReceiveMessage request,
8
and therefore, a message will be returned from the queue.
9
Now the visibility timeout begins.
10
And by default, that message visibility timeout
11
is 30 seconds.
12
That means that during these 30 seconds,
13
the message has to be processed, okay?
14
And if you do so,
15
that means that if the same or other consumers
16
do a message request API call,
17
then the message will not be returned.
18
And again another one during the timeout window,
19
the message will not be returned.
20
So effectively, during the visibility timeout,
21
that message is invisible to other consumers.
22
But after the visibility timeout is elapsed
23
and if the message has not been deleted,
24
then the message will be
25
quote unquote put back into the queue
26
and therefore, another consumer or the same consumer
27
doing a receive message API call
28
will receive the message again, the same message as before.
29
So, this is something that's really important to understand.
30
As you can see, while we receive a message,
31
it becomes invisible during the visibility timeout period.
32
Now, if we take a look at the same diagram,
33
what we notice is that
34
if we don't process a message
35
within the visibility timeout window,
36
then it will be processed twice potentially, right?
37
Because it will be received by two different consumers,
38
or twice by the same consumer.
39
And so, if a consumer is actively processing a message
40
but knows that it needs a bit more time
41
to process the message because otherwise,
42
it will go out of the visibility timeout window,
43
there is an API called ChangeMessageVisibility.
44
And so if a consumer knows
45
that a message needs a bit more time to be processed
46
and you don't want to process that message twice,
47
then the consumer should call
48
the ChangeMessageVisibility API to tell SQS,
49
hey, do not make that message visible for now, okay?
50
I just need a bit more time to process this message.
51
And so, how do you set this message visibility timeout?
52
Well, if you set it to
53
a really, really high value by default, say, hours,
54
and the consumer crashes,
55
then it will take hours until this message reappears,
56
re-becomes visible in your SQS queue,
57
and that will take a lot of time.
58
If you set it to something really, really low,
59
like a few seconds,
60
what happens that if the consumer
61
doesn't end up having enough time to process that message
62
for whatever reason,
63
then it will be read many times by different consumers
64

65
So the idea is that the visibility timeout
66

of that visibility window.

--- SQS - Long Polling ---

1
So let's go ahead
2
and discuss long polling in Amazon SQS.
3
So the idea that your consumer,
4
that is requesting messages from the queue,
5
and it can wait for the messages to arrive,
6
if, when you do a request,
7
there are no messages for now in the queue.
8
This is called long polling.
9
So you have a queue
10
and then your consumer is going to poll the queue,
11
but the consumer can wait for a message to arrive.
12
So a message is going to arrive.
13
And then when, as soon as the message arrives,
14
it's going to be sent to the consumer.
15
So the idea is that with the long polling,
16
your consumer is going to decrease the number of API calls,
17
because they are long API calls.
18
Your consumer is asking SQS Queue maybe
19
for 10 seconds for a message.
20
And also, while you have less API calls,
21
you're going to also reduce the latency of your application.
22
Why?
23
Well, because as soon as a message is received by SQS,
24
it is going to be sent to the consumer.
25
And so therefore your consumer will receive your messages
26
with the least amount of lag.
27
So the long polling can be set anywhere between one second
28
to 20 seconds, and obviously, the longer you wait,
29
the more efficient you're going to do
30
and the less API calls you're going to do to SQS.
31
So, a wait time of 20 seconds may be preferable.
32
So overall you should prefer long polling to short polling,
33
and you can enable this at the queue level
34
or at the API level using the WaitTimeSeconds parameters.
35
Okay, so that's it for this lecture, I hope you liked it.
36
And I will see you in the next lecture.

--- SNS and SQS -  Fan Out Pattern ---

1
Now let's talk about
2
the SNS plus SQS fan-out pattern.
3
The idea is that you want a message
4
to be sent to multiple SQS queues,
5
but if you send them individually to every SQS queue,
6
there can be problems associated with it.
7
For example, if your application crashes in between,
8
if there are delivery failures,
9
or if you add more SQS queues down the road.
10
Therefore we want to use the fan-out pattern.
11
The idea is that you're going to push once an SNS topic
12
and then you're going to subscribe as many SQS queues
13
as you want to the SNS topic.
14
These queues are subscribers
15
and they will all receive the messages sent into SNS.
16
So for example, we have a buying service
17
that wants to send messages to two SQS queues.
18
What it will do instead,
19
it will send one message into an SNS topic,
20
and the queues are subscribers of that SNS topic
21
so that the fraud service and the shipping service
22
can read all messages from their own SQS queues.
23
The idea with this as well
24
is that it's a fully decoupled model
25
and there is no data loss.
26
SQS will give you data persistence, delayed processing,
27
as well as retries of work.
28
And with this pattern, we can add more SQS queues
29
as a subscriber of the SNS topic over time.
30
For this, we need to make sure
31
that your SQS queue access policy,
32
as we've seen from before,
33
allows your SNS topic to write to your SQS queue.
34
So again, yet another use case
35
for using queue access policies,
36
and we have cross-region delivery.
37
So it's definitely possible for an SNS topic
38
in one region to send messages
39
to SQS queues in other regions if the security allows it.

--- Amazon Data Firehose ---

1
So now let's talk about Amazon Data Firehose.
2
So Amazon Data Firehose is a service
3
to send data from sources into target destinations.
4
So to get data into Amazon Data Firehose,
5
you may have producers that could be your applications,
6
your clients, or things you write,
7
and you use the SDK to send data into Firehose
8
or the Kinesis agents,
9
as well as Firehose has the capability
10
to pull directly from some services
11
such as, for example, a Kinesis Data Streams
12
or an Amazon CloudWatch logs and events,
13
or for example, AWS IoT.
14
And so all these services are either going
15
to be pushing into Amazon Data Firehose
16
or Firehose are going to be pulling from,
17
for example, a Kinesis data stream
18
and it is going to receive the records.
19
Now these records are going to be received,
20
and then they can optionally be transformed
21
using a Lambda function, if you wanted
22
to do some data conversion format, for example.
23
And they're going to be accumulated into a buffer
24
and the buffer is going to be flushed once in a while
25
to do batch writing into a lot of destinations.
26
So the first destinations are going
27
to be AWS specific destinations,
28
such as sending data into Amazon S3
29
or into Amazon Redshift to perform analytics,
30
or into Amazon OpenSearch as well.
31
You also have the option to send from Data Firehose
32
directly into third-party partner destinations
33
such as Datadog, Splunk, New Relic, and MongoDB.
34
And finally, if your destination is not supported,
35
you can simply use the HTTP endpoint integration
36
to send it anywhere you want.
37
Now, Firehose will write this data,
38
but you also have the option to write all
39
or just the failed data that has been sent
40
into an S3 bucket for a backup.
41
So Amazon Data Firehose
42
used to be called Kinesis Data Firehose
43
for the longest time,
44
but now it's called Amazon Data Firehose
45
because it does way more than just Kinesis.
46
It's a fully managed service,
47
and again, it supports Redshift, S3,
48
and Amazon OpenSearch service,
49
third party destinations such as Splunk
50
and a custom HTTP endpoint
51
if you wanted to write your own integration.
52
You also have automatic scaling.
53
It's fully serverless,
54
and you only pay for what you use from within the service.
55
It's called a near real-time service
56
and this is something you have to look for in the exam.
57
Near real-time usually points
58
to Amazon Data Firehose, and why?
59
Well, because you have a buffer inside of Firehose,
60
and the buffer can be optionally disabled,
61
but usually it's used
62
and it has a capability based on size or time.
63
So it's going to accumulate, accumulate,
64
and then after a while,

it's going to be flushed into your destination.

And therefore, because that takes a little bit of time,
67
it's a near real-time service.

For example, if you wanted to change your data

to write your own producer and consumer code.

For Amazon Data Firehose,

--- SQS vs SNS vs Kinesis ---

1
Okay.
2
So it's very important that you understand
3
the difference between SQS, SNS and Kinesis.
4
So SQS has a model where consumers pull data
5
by requesting messages from the SQSQ.
6
And once the data is processed
7
then the consumer has to delete it from the queue
8
so that's no other consumers can read it ever again.
9
You can have as many workers as you want.
10
So as many consumers as you want
11
and they all work together to consume
12
and delete all the messages from the queue.
13
You don't need to provision throughput in advance
14
because it is a managed service
15
and it can scale to hundreds of thousands
16
of messages very quickly.
17
The ordering guarantees are only available
18
if you enable FIFO queues.
19
So first it in first out type of queues.
20
And you also have individual message delay capability
21
if you want a message to appear to a consumer in the queue
22
after a certain amount of time, for example, 30 seconds.
23
When you look at SNS, this is a different model.
24
This is a pup sub model.
25
So you push data to many subscribers
26
and they will all receive a copy
27
of the message you're sending.
28
You can get up to 12,500,000 subscribers per SNS topic.
29
And once the data is sent to SNS, it is not persistent.
30
That means that if it is not delivered
31
you have a chance of losing it.
32
So it's a pub, as I said
33
and you can scale to hundreds of thousands of topics.
34
You don't need to provision throughput as well.
35
And if you want to combine it with SQS, you can.
36
So using the fan out architecture pattern
37
you can combine SNS with SQS
38
or you can combine SNS FIFO topics with SQS FIFO queues.
39
Okay.
40
Now finally, Kinesis has two modes of consumption.
41
You have the standard mode
42
where consumers pull data from Kinesis.
43
In which case you get two megabytes per second, per shard
44
or if you have enhanced fan out type
45
of consumption mechanism, you have Kinesis, sorry,
46
that pushes data into your consumers.
47
In which case you get two megabytes per second, per shard
48
per consumer, which gives you a much higher throughput
49
and the ability to have much more applications reading
50
from your Kinesis stream.
51
You have the possibility to reply data
52
because the data is persisted with new Kinesis data stream.
53
And so Kinesis is going to be used for real time big data,
54
analytics and ETL.
55
You will get ordering at the shard level
56
and you have to specify how many shards you want
57
per Kinesis data stream in advance.
58
So you need to scale the shard yourself
59
and the data will expire after X days.
60
And at the time of recording
61
this is between one and 365 days of data retention.
62
In terms of capacity mode,
63
we have two modes, the provision mode
64
in which we specify in advance the amount of shards we want
65
for Kinesis streams or the on-demand capacity mode,
66
where the number of shard is adjusted
67
by Kinesis streams directly for us.
68
Okay.
69
So that's it for this summer lecture.

I hope you liked it.

And I will see you in the next lecture.

--- Amazon MQ ---

1
So now let's talk about Amazon MQ.
2
So we know about SQS and SNS
3
and they're cloud-native services
4
because they are proprietary protocols from AWS.
5
They use their own sets of APIs.
6
But if you are running traditional application on-premises,
7
you may use open protocols
8
such as MQTT, AMQP, STOMP, Openwire, WSS.
9
And when you're migrating your application to the cloud,
10
you may not want to re-engineer your application
11
to use the SQS and the SNS protocols or APIs.
12
So instead, you wanna use the traditional protocols
13
you used to, such as MQTT, AMQP, and so on.
14
So for this, we can use Amazon MQ.
15
So Amazon MQ is very simple.
16
It's a managed message broker service for two technologies,
17
for RabbitMQ and for ActiveMQ.
18
So RabbitMQ and ActiveMQ are, for example,
19
on-premises technologies that provide you access
20
to the open protocols I just mentioned.
21
So then we can get a managed version of these brokers
22
onto the cloud thanks to Amazon MQ.
23
So as such, you can understand the implications.
24
First of all, Amazon MQ doesn't scale as much as SQS or SNS,
25
which have sort of like infinite scaling.
26
And because Amazon MQ runs on servers,
27
you may have server issues.
28
And so you can run multi-AZ setup
29
with a failover if you want to be highly available.
30
Also, Amazon MQ comes with both a queue feature,
31
so it looks like SQS,
32
and topic features, it looks like SNS
33
as part of a single broker.
34
Now, how does the high availability work for Amazon MQ?
35
Well, for example, let's say we have a region us-east-1
36
and we have two availability zones,
37
us-east-1a and us-east-1b.
38
One zone is going to be active
39
and the other one is going to be a standby.
40
So we're going to have an Amazon MQ broker in both AZ, okay,
41
where one is active and one is standby.
42
And so for the failover to work,
43
you need to define Amazon EFS as your backend storage.
44
And we've seen that EFS is a network file system
45
which can be mounted onto multiple availability zones.
46
So what happens is that whenever
47
you have failover happening,
48
well, the standby is going to be also mounted
49
onto Amazon EFS, and therefore will have the same data
50
as your first active queue
51
and therefore the failover can happen correctly.
52
So if your client talks to the Amazon MQ broker, okay,
53
and there is a failover happening,
54
then the data will be kept safe thanks to Amazon EFS.
55
And that's it.
56
That's all you need to remember for going to the exam.
57
I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

--- Amazon ECS - Auto Scaling ---

1
So now let's talk
2
about ECS Service Auto Scaling.
3
So as we can see, we can manually increase
4
the number of ECS tasks in our service.
5
But we can also automatically increase
6
or decrease the number of tasks.
7
For this, we can leverage the service
8
called the AWS Application Auto Scaling.
9
And we have three metrics we can scale on using the service.
10
We can scale on the CPU Utilization of the ECS Service.
11
We can scale on the Memory Utilization,
12
which is the RAM of the ECS Service.
13
Or, the ALB Request Count Per Target,
14
which is a metric coming from the ALB.
15
So only these metrics you have to remember.
16
Then, you can set up different kind of auto scaling.
17
You can set up Target Tracking to track
18
for a specific target for the three metrics shown above.
19
Or Step Scaling.
20
Or Scheduled Scaling,
21
if you wanted to scale your ECS Service ahead of time
22
thanks to predictable changes.
23
Remember, that scaling your service, your ECS Service,
24
at the task level is not equal to scaling your cluster
25
of EC2 instances if you are in the EC2 launch type.
26
And so therefore, that's why when you don't
27
have an EC2 auto scaling that's necessary,
28
when you don't have EC2 instances in the backend,
29
then using Fargate makes service auto scaling much easier
30
to set up, because everything is serverless.
31
And it's why I'm fan of Fargate.
32
And the exam is pushing you to use Fargate a lot.
33
So for the EC2 launch type,
34
how can we actually scale the EC2 instances
35
in the backend if we're using it?
36
So we have multiple ways of doing it.
37
We can use an Auto Scaling Group Scaling.
38
And so we scale our ASG, for example,
39
based on CPU Utilization.
40
And then we can add EC2 instance over time
41
if the CPU skyrockets.
42
Or, we can use the newer and more advanced feature
43
called the ECS Cluster Capacity Provider
44
that we've seen before in the hands-on.
45
And with this one, the Capacity Provider is very smart.
46
And as soon as you lack capacity to launch new tasks,
47
it's going to automatically scale your ASG.
48
So the Capacity Provider is paired
49
with a Auto Scaling Group.
50
And then when you're missing RAM or CPU,
51
there you go, EC2 instances are created.
52
And so the second option is the smarter way of doing things.
53
So if you have to choose between Auto Scaling Group Scaling
54
and ECS Cluster Capacity Provider,
55
please use ECS Cluster Capacity Provider
56
for your EC2 launch type.
57
So let's have a look at the service.
58
So we have a Service A with two tasks.
59
And we have CPU Usage.
60
And it's going to be auto scaled
61
by the AWS Application Auto Scaling.
62
But let's assume we have more users,
63
and therefore your CPU usage goes really up,
64
then your CloudWatch Metric,
65
which monitors the CPU Usage at the ECS service level again,
66
is going to trigger a CloudWatch Alarm,
67
which will trigger a scaling activity
68
in your Auto Scaling for your ECS service.
69
The desired capacity will increase
70
for your ECS Service, and a new task will be created.
71
And optionally, if this service is running
72
on the EC2 launch type,
73
then the ECS Capacity Providers
74
can help you scale your ECS cluster
75
backed by EC2 instances.

--- Amazon ECS - Solutions Architectures ---

1
Now let's talk about
2
a few solution architectures
3
you can encounter with Amazon ECS.
4
So the first one are ECS tasks invoked by Event Bridge.
5
So for example, say we have an Amazon ECS cluster,
6
it's backed by Fargate, and we have S3 buckets.
7
Our users are going to upload objects into our S3 buckets,
8
And these S3 buckets can be, for example,
9
integrated with Amazon Event Bridge
10
to send all the events to it.
11
And Amazon Event Bridge can have a rule
12
to run ECS tasks on the go.
13
Now, when ECS tasks are going to be created,
14
they will have an ECS task role associated with them,
15
and from the task itself
16
what it can do is that it can get the objects, process it,
17
and then send the results into Amazon DynamoDB.
18
And that is thanks to the fact
19
that we have an ECS task role associated with it.
20
And so effectively here, what we've done
21
is that we've created a serverless architecture
22
to process images, or to process objects,
23
from your S3 buckets using a Docker container.
24
And that is using Amazon Event Bridge ECS
25
in the Fargate mode, as well as an ECS task role
26
to talk to Amazon S3 and Amazon DynamoDB.
27
Another architecture using, again, Event Bridge,
28
is to use an Event Bridge schedule.
29
So we have an Amazon ECS cluster
30
backed by Fargate and Amazon Event Bridge,
31
and we schedule a rule to be triggered every 1 hour.
32
Now, this rule is going to run ECS tasks for us in Fargate,
33
and so that means that every 1 hour,
34
a new task will be created in our Fargate cluster,
35
and the task can do whatever we want.
36
For example, we can create an ECS task role
37
with access to Amazon S3, and therefore our task,
38
our Docker container, our program can, for example,
39
do every 1 hour some batch processing
40
against some files in Amazon S3.
41
And again, all of that architecture is fully serverless.
42
A last example is using ECS and an SQS queue,
43
so we could have a service on ECS with two ECS tasks,
44
and messages are being sent into an SQS queue,
45
and the service itself is pulling for messages
46
from the SQS queue, and processing them.
47
We can enable ECS Service Auto Scaling
48
on top of this service.
49
That means that, for example, the more messages we have
50
in our SQS queue, the more tasks we're going to have
51
into our ECS service, thanks to auto-scaling.
52
Another integration is when you want to use Event Bridge
53
to actually intercept events from within your ECS cluster.
54
So, for example, say you wanted to react
55
to tasks being exited.
56
In that case, any task exiting or starting
57
in your ECS cluster can be triggered as an event
58
in Event Bridge, and it will look like this.
59
For example, the ECS task state change for "stopped"
60
and the stopped reason.
61
Then from there, for example, we could alert an SNS topic
62
and send emails to your administrators.
63
So, bottom line, Event Bridge does allow you to understand
64
the lifecycle of your containers in your ECS cluster.
65
Okay, so that's it for this lecture.

I hope you liked it, and I will see you in the next lecture.

--- Amazon Cognito Overview ---

1
So now let's talk about Amazon Cognito.
2
And the goal of it is to give user an identity
3
to interact with a web and mobile application.
4
So these users usually sit outside of our AWS account,
5
hence the name Cognito,
6
because it gives an identity to users
7
that we don't know about yet.
8
So we have two kind of sub-services within Cognito.
9
We have the Cognito user pool,
10
and this provides a sign-in functionality
11
for app users and has really good integration
12
with API Gateway and the Application Load Balancer.
13
And we have the Cognito Identity Pool,
14
used to be called Federated Identity.
15
And this is to actually provide temporary AWS credentials
16
to users that are registered with their application
17
so that they can access some resources of AWS directly.
18
And there is a good integration
19
as we'll see with Cognito User Pools.
20
So if you are asking yourself,
21
"Don't we already have users in IAM?"

The answer is yes, you do,
23
but Cognito is gonna be for your web

and mobile application users,

which sits outside of AWS.

So look for the keyword,
27
such as hundreds of users, or mobile users,
28
or authentication with whatever mechanism
29
such as SAML and so on.
30
So let's do a deep dive into Cognito User Pool or CUP.
31
So it's a serverless database of users
32
for your web and mobile application.
33
And you can define a simple login,
34
such as username or email and a password as a combination.

You have password reset feature.

You can have email and phone number verification,

multi-factor authentication for users,

and you can also have integration with,

for example, Facebook for your login,

So this Cognito User Pools,

they integrate with the API Gateway

So if we take the example of the API Gateway,

And now your lambda function knows

with your Cognito User Pool

So that means that your application

So this really allows you

So it's a responsibility that you've moved

that is going to balance the load for your backend.

So the API Gateway or the ALB.

Okay, the other sub-part of Cognito is

And it's to get identities for users, but this time,

they don't access our application

through the API Gateway or the Application Load Balancer,

but instead, they're going to directly access

your AWS accounts using temporary AWS credentials.

So the users' source can be, for example,

and then they can access the services

of AWS directly or through the API Gateway.

So the IAM policies applied to the credentials are defined

within the Cognito Identity Pool service already.

And they can be customized

And in case you want to have a default IAM role, you can,

so that your guest users or authenticated users

that don't have specific roles defined to them

will inherit this defined IAM role.

So a diagram will surely help you

to understand what identity pools are.

So let's say your web and mobile applications

want to have direct access

into an S3 bucket or DynamoDB table.

So we're going to have Cognito Identity Pools for this.

So the web and mobile application is

going to log in and get a token out of it.

So it could be a login against Cognito User Pools,

or social identity provider,

or SAML, or open ID connect and so on.

And then it's going to take this token

And this enables for you a use case

So you would, for example,

have this policy coming out of the Cognito Identity Pools.

And the idea is that in it, you have a condition,

and this condition is saying

--- Organizations - Overview ---

1
So now let's talk about AWS Organizations.
2
So it's a global service
3
and it allows you to manage multiple AWS accounts
4
at the same time.
5
So you create an organization
6
and the main account in your organization
7
is called the management account,
8
while the other accounts that join the organization
9
or that are created from the organizations
10
are called member accounts.
11
And remember, accounts can only be part of one organization.
12
The cool thing about organization
13
is that the billing is consolidated
14
across all the accounts.
15
So you have a single payment method
16
on the management account
17
and then it will be paying for all the organization's cost.
18
But because you have an organization
19
and it's all part of one big family,
20
then you get pricing benefits from aggregated usage.
21
So if you use a lot EC2 or if you use a lot Amazon S3
22
across all your accounts,
23
then you will get big discounts,
24
because it will summarize and sum up
25
all the usage across all the accounts.
26
You can also share reserved instances
27
and saving plans discounts across accounts.
28
So if a reserved instance is unused in one account,
29
another account can benefit from it
30
and therefor the discounts apply
31
across the entire organization,
32
which is really good for cost savings.
33
Now, there's also an API
34
to automate the account creation
35
from within the organization.
36
So you can create accounts very easily
37
using an organization.
38
So how does that work?
39
So we have what's called a root organizational unit, or OU,
40
and this is the outermost OU of your accounts
41
and then within it sits the management account.
42
Then you can create sub-OUs,

so you can create for example an OU for the dev accounts
44
and then you can create member accounts within the dev OU
45
or you can create OU for a prod account

and also add member accounts there,

You can create within the prod OU,

an OU for your HR member accounts

So you can organize it the way you want.

so you have for example,
55

and then different accounts within each OU.

so for example, one OU for prod,
60
one OU for test, one OU for dev
61
and within each OU, some accounts.
62
Or project-based, so you can have an OU per project
63
within an account, within each project.
64
And you can mix and match.
65
You're really free to do whatever you want.

So what are the advantages of using organizations?
67
Well, thanks to having multiple accounts,
68
you can have better security
69
versus having one account with multiple VPC,

because accounts are more separated than VPCs.

for billing purposes
73
and you can in one go, enable CloudTrail

for all your accounts
75
and send all the logs into a central S3 account,

or we can also send CloudWatch logs
77
to a central logging account
78
and we can establish cross account roles
79

80
So we can administer all the other accounts
81
from the management account.
82
So these are big advantages.
83
Also, there's a big security advantage.
84

and it's an IAM policy applied to specific OUs or accounts
86
and this allows you to restrict
87
what the users and roles all of them can do
88
within the accounts.

--- IAM - Resource-based Policies vs IAM Roles ---

1
So let's have a look now
2
at the fundamental differences
3
between IAM roles and resource-based policies.
4
So for cross accounts,
5
especially when you want to perform an API call
6
on an S3 bucket cross account,
7
you have two options.
8
You can attach a resource-based policy to a resource,
9
for example, an S3 bucket policy on an S3 bucket,
10
or you can decide to use a role
11
that can actually access the resource.
12
So let's take an example of these two options.
13
So this is the example
14
where the user in Account A can assume a role in Account B,
15
and that role has the permissions
16
to access your Amazon S3 buckets.
17
Or similarly, the user in Account A,
18
through a bucket policy placed on the Amazon S3 bucket
19
in Account B,
20
can access the S3 buckets.
21
So both these two situations are valid,
22
but there is a little bit of difference, okay?
23
The first one is an IAM role
24
that has access to the S3 bucket.
25
The second one is the S3 bucket policy that allows the user.
26
So what's the difference?
27
When you actually assume a role, okay,
28
you actually give up all your original permissions,
29
and you take all the permissions assigned to the role.
30
So this is very important.
31
That means that we, for example, assume a role,
32
and this role can do whatever.
33
We can now do anything that the role does,
34
but we cannot use our original permissions.
35
And so when you use a resource-based policy,
36
instead, the principal does not assume a role,
37
and therefore, he does not have to give up his permissions.
38
So if you take an example of user in Account A,
39
they need to scan a DynamoDB table in Account A,
40
and then dump it in an S3 bucket in Account B.
41
What they can do is we should use a resource-based policy
42
because this way, we don't have to assume a role,
43
and we can both scan the DynamoDB table
44
and write to an S3 bucket in another account.
45
So resource-based policies are supported
46
by more and more AWS services and resources over time.
47
So we have the Amazon S3 buckets, the SNS topics,
48
the SQS queues, the Lambda functions, and so on.
49
And the big difference of when this comes into play
50
is when you use Amazon EventBridge.
51
So when an EventBridge rule runs,
52
it's going to need permissions on the targets.
53
And if your target supports resource-based policies,
54
for example, Lambda functions, SNS topics,
55
SQS queues, S3 buckets, or API Gateway,
56
then it's possible that EventBridge
57
will just add a resource-based policy on the target
58
to allow the invocation from the EventBridge rule.
59
That's one case.
60
On the other hand,
61
if the resource doesn't necessarily support
62
a resource policy,
63
then EventBridge will use an IAM role
64
to invoke the target service,
65
for example, for Kinesis Stream, EC2 Auto Scaling,
66
System Manager Run Command, ECS task, and so on.
67
And for example, for Kinesis Data Streams,
68
as a note, it supports resource-based policies,
69
but still, EventBridge is going to use an IAM role.
70
So how do you know which one is going to be used in which?
71
Well, you need to look at the configuration
72
of the EventBridge role itself
73
to see how this is going to work,
74
and then you will know, okay?
75
But as a matter of fact, Lambda, SNS, SQS,
76
S3 buckets are using resource-based policies.
77
And Kinesis Data Streams, EC2 Auto Scaling,
78
and so on are using IAM roles.
79
Even though it's possible
80
for you to use a resource-based policy
81
with Kinesis Data Stream,
82
that's not yet supported by EventBridge.
83
So all the information you need to know

for the exam is on this slide,

and I know that'll be enough for you at the exam.
